name: Achaicus
title: Christian messenger from Corinth
summary: Achaicus was a believer from the church in Corinth who, together with Stephanas and Fortunatus, traveled to Ephesus to visit the apostle Paul. The trio brought news and likely a letter from the Corinthian church containing questions that Paul answers in his first letter to the Corinthians. Paul describes their visit as a refreshment for his spirit and urges the Corinthian church to show appreciation toward such faithful coworkers. Achaicus' service illustrates how fellowship in the early church was maintained through personal messengers who connected congregations across great distances.

keyEvents.title: Visit to Paul in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: Achaicus traveled with Stephanas and Fortunatus from Corinth to Ephesus to visit Paul. They likely brought a letter from the church containing questions that Paul answers in his first letter to the Corinthians.

keyEvents.title: Refreshment for Paul's spirit
keyEvents.description: Paul testifies that Achaicus and his companions brought great joy and refreshment to his spirit through their presence and their report from the church in Corinth. Paul urges the Corinthians to recognize such faithful coworkers.

versions.summary: Achaicus was a Christian from Corinth who, together with Stephanas and Fortunatus, visited the apostle Paul in Ephesus. He brought important news from the church in Corinth and was a great encouragement to Paul. His name means 'from Achaia' and indicates his Greek background.

versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Messenger from Corinth' is clear, but could be made slightly more precise by including that he was a Christian co-worker. 'Messenger' still adequately covers his role.; [minor] The role 'servant' is somewhat vague. Epaphroditus is primarily described as a messenger and church delegate. The roles 'messenger' and 'church envoy' would have been more precise descriptions of his function.; [minor] The third key event element 'Recognition from Paul' refers to verse 18, but the call to recognize such men is found in verses 16:18-18 and especially verse 16:16. Verse 16:18 concerns how they refreshed Paul's spirit, while the call for recognition is more broadly present at the conclusion of the chapter.; [major] Footnotes are missing. There are interesting linguistic and historical points about Epaphroditus: his name, possible slave background, and the role of the delegation in the early church.

footnotes.text: The name Achaicus (Greek: Ἀχαϊκός) means 'belonging to Achaia', the Roman province that included southern Greece with Corinth as its capital. The name was common among freed slaves and may indicate that Achaicus or his ancestors had a slave background in the region.

The delegation consisting of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus likely brought the letter from the Corinthians that Paul refers to in 1 Cor 7:1 ('Now concerning what you wrote...'). They thus served as official church representatives, an important role in the early church's communication system.

That Paul uses the expression 'they refreshed my spirit' (1 Cor 16:18) about Achaicus and his traveling companions shows that personal contact and oral reports were invaluable in the early church, where long-distance communication was difficult and costly.

Fortunatus and Achaicus are names often associated with the Roman slave class. Clement of Rome (c. 96 AD) mentions a Fortunatus in his letter to the Corinthians, which has led to speculation about possible connections to the same Christian community in Corinth.

Corinth was during Paul's time one of the most important cities in the eastern Roman Empire, rebuilt as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. The city was known for its cosmopolitan character and large population of freed slaves, which is reflected in the names of several members of the church.
